title: Ground-State Properties of a Lattice-Coupled Strongly Correlated Model for Solid Oxygen under Pressure
authors: Naomichi Sato, Makoto Naka, Joji Nasu
abstract: Solid oxygen is an $S=1$ molecular magnet with strong   coupling between spin and lattice degrees of freedom.   Recent studies suggest that magnetic moments   coexist with tetramer distortions under pressure.   We derive an effective spin Hamiltonian from a two-orbital   Peierls--Hubbard model with spin-orbit coupling.   The resulting model contains competing easy-plane   single-ion and easy-axis exchange anisotropies.   We analyze this model on a square lattice using quantum Monte Carlo simulations   and evaluate the magnetic contribution to the lattice stiffness   for several lattice distortion patterns including the tetramer pattern.   We find that the tetramer pattern is the most favorable   among the considered distortion patterns throughout the parameter range studied.   Moreover, competition between the two anisotropies   enhances the tendency toward lattice distortion   and strengthens the preference for tetramerization over the other patterns.
summary: This work models solid oxygen, an $S=1$ magnet, using an effective spin Hamiltonian derived from a Hubbard-like model. By simulating the magnetic contribution to lattice stiffness, the authors determine that the tetramer distortion is the most stable structure. They show that the competition between different magnetic anisotropies actively drives and strengthens this preference for tetramerization.
main_problem: The study investigates the microscopic magnetic mechanism that favors specific lattice distortion patterns, particularly tetramerization, in solid oxygen under pressure.
main_result: The tetramer pattern is consistently found to be the most favorable distortion pattern across the studied parameter range, and the competition between different spin anisotropies enhances this tendency.
method: Quantum Monte Carlo simulations are employed to calculate the magnetic contribution to the lattice stiffness, which determines the stability of various distortion patterns.
model_or_system: The system is solid oxygen, modeled using an effective S=1 spin Hamiltonian derived from a two-orbital Peierls–Hubbard model incorporating spin-orbit coupling. This Hamiltonian includes competing easy-plane and easy-axis anisotropies.
key_observables: The magnetic contribution to the lattice stiffness ($a_\eta$) for zigzag, meander, and tetramer patterns, and the difference in this contribution ($\Delta a_\eta$).
important_parameters: The ratios of single-ion anisotropy ($D_0/J$) and uniaxial exchange anisotropy ($J_{z2}/J$), and the lattice distortion amplitude ($\delta$).
main_assumptions: The analysis operates in the strong-coupling regime, and certain terms ($\Delta H$) are neglected due to small energy scales.
figures_summary: Figure 2 shows the magnetic contributions $a_\eta$ to the lattice stiffness per site as a function of $J_{z^2}/J$ for the three distortion patterns at fixed ratios of $D_0/J$.
paper_structure: The paper derives an effective spin Hamiltonian, calculates the magnetic contribution to the lattice stiffness using QMC simulations, and systematically compares the stability of zigzag, meander, and tetramer patterns based on the calculated $a_\eta$ values.
why_interesting: The coupling between magnetic ordering (spin anisotropy) and structural instability (lattice distortion) is a core theme in strongly correlated materials, making this relevant for understanding emergent quantum phases.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. (a) Two-dimensional square lattice representing the molecular arrangement in the ab plane of solid oxygen. Each site represents an O2 molecule. The four sublattices A, B, C, and D, the eight nearest- neighbor bond types b1, . . . , b8, and the coordinate axes are indicated. (b) Zigzag, (c) meander, and (d) tetramer distortion patterns whose relative stability is examined in this study. Solid and dashed lines denote bond modulations +δ/2 and −δ/2, respectively. With the components ordered according to b1, . . . , b8, the corresponding modulation vectors are vZ = (1, −1, 1, −1, −1, 1, −1, 1), vM = (1, −1, 1, −1, 1, −1, −1, 1), and vT = (1, −1, 1, −1, 1, −1, 1, −1).

Fig. 2. (a)–(c) Magnetic contributions aη to the lattice stiffness per site as functions of Jz2/J for D0/J = 0.0, 0.2, and 0.4, respectively. The symbols represent the zigzag (red), meander (blue), and tetramer (green) patterns. (d)–(f) Bare term ∆abare η and response term ∆aresponse η in the differences relative to the tetramer pattern for the same values of D0/J as in (a)–(c). Circles and squares denote the response and bare contributions, respectively. The bare contributions overlap at zero. All values and their differences are expressed in units of J.

Fig. 3. (a) Mean-square z component of the spin, ⟨(S z)2⟩. (b) Bare and (c) response terms in the magnetic contribution to the lattice stiffness per site for the tetramer pattern. These terms are expressed in units of J. All quantities are evaluated in the undistorted system and plotted as functions of Jz2/J. Black, orange, and purple symbols correspond to D0/J = 0.0, 0.2, and 0.4, respectively.
